los.text: Describe the main causes, symptoms, clinical signs, investigation, pathophysiology and principles of treatment/management of pleural disease
sessions: Clin 2: Clinical assessment of pleural disease
Clin 3: Workup and management of pleural disease
Clin 4: Workup and management of pneumothorax
los.html:
Pleuritic chest pain

  • Sharp, worse on inspiration/cough. Causes: PE, pneumonia, pneumothorax, viral pleurisy, autoimmune (SLE, RA), malignancy, rib fracture, pericarditis.

Pleural effusion

Signs↓ expansion, stony dull percussion, ↓ breath sounds and vocal resonance; tracheal deviation away if large.
IxCXR (blunted costophrenic angle, meniscus), ultrasound (guides tap), diagnostic aspiration: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cytology, MC&S. CT if malignancy suspected.
Light's criteria → exudate if any: fluid/serum protein >0.5, fluid/serum LDH >0.6, fluid LDH >⅔ upper limit of normal serum LDH.
Transudate (↑ hydrostatic / ↓ oncotic)Exudate (↑ permeability / ↓ lymph drainage)
Heart failure (commonest), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia, hypothyroidism, Meigs'Parapneumonic/empyema, malignancy, TB, PE, RA/SLE, pancreatitis
  • Mx: treat cause.
    • Therapeutic aspiration for breathlessness.
    • Chest drain if empyema (pus, or pH <7.2).
    • Recurrent malignant effusion: pleurodesis or indwelling pleural catheter.

Pneumothorax

  • Primary (tall thin young males, smokers, apical blebs) vs secondary (COPD, CF, asthma, TB).
  • Sudden pleuritic pain + breathlessness
  • ↓ breath sounds, hyper-resonant.
IxErect CXR (visible visceral pleural line, absent lung markings).
Mx (BTS 2023)
  • If minimal symptoms → conservative/ambulatory
  • If symptomatic → needle aspiration or chest drain
  • Secondary pneumothorax usually admitted for drain.
  • Advise no flying until resolved
  • Never dive unless definitive surgery.
Tension pneumothorax: haemodynamic compromise, tracheal deviation away, ↑JVP. Clinical diagnosis → immediate decompression (2nd ICS MCL or 4th/5th ICS mid-axillary line), then chest drain.

los.text: Describe the mechanisms by which drugs produce therapeutic effects in the body (pharmacodynamics), including synergism, antagonism and drug interactions
los.html:
PharmacodynamicsWhat the drug does to the body: drug–target interaction and response.
TargetsReceptors (ion channels, GPCRs, kinase-linked, nuclear), enzymes, transporters, ion channels.
AgonistAffinity + efficacy. Partial agonist (e.g. buprenorphine): submaximal effect, can antagonise full agonists. Inverse agonist: reduces constitutive activity.
Antagonists
  • Competitive (reversible, surmountable; shifts dose–response curve right, same max: e.g. naloxone, atropine)
  • Non-competitive/irreversible (↓ maximum: e.g. aspirin on COX, phenoxybenzamine).
  • Physiological antagonism: opposing actions via different receptors (adrenaline vs histamine).
  • Chemical: e.g. protamine binds heparin.
Potency (EC50) vs efficacy (Emax). Therapeutic index = TD50/ED50 (narrow: warfarin, digoxin, lithium, gentamicin).
Synergism
  • Combined effect > sum (e.g. trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole; opioid + benzodiazepine respiratory depression).
  • Additive: = sum.
  • Potentiation: one drug increases another's effect without its own action.
InteractionsPharmacokinetic (one drug alters ADME of another: CYP inhibition/induction, protein binding, renal excretion) vs pharmacodynamic (combined effects at targets: e.g. two QT-prolonging drugs, NSAID + anticoagulant bleeding).
Tolerance/tachyphylaxisReceptor desensitisation/downregulation (nitrates, opioids, β-agonists).

los.text: Explain the control of respiration including the functions of the main respiratory centres in the brainstem
los.html:
Brainstem centres
  • Medulla: dorsal respiratory group (inspiration; receives vagal/glossopharyngeal input via NTS) and ventral respiratory group (inspiratory and expiratory neurons for forced breathing). Pre-Bötzinger complex = rhythm generator.
  • Pons: pneumotaxic centre (inhibits inspiration, ↑ rate) and apneustic centre (prolongs inspiration).
Central chemoreceptors(ventral medulla)Respond to CSF H⁺ from CO₂ crossing the BBB. Main driver of ventilation (~70% of response to CO₂).
Peripheral chemoreceptors(carotid bodies via CN IX; aortic bodies via CN X)Respond to ↓PaO₂ (below ~8 kPa), ↑PaCO₂ and ↑H⁺ (metabolic acidosis).
Lung receptorsStretch (Hering–Breuer reflex), irritant (cough, bronchoconstriction), J receptors (pulmonary congestion → dyspnoea).
CortexVoluntary control (speech, breath-holding); limbic input (anxiety).
  • In chronic CO₂ retention (some COPD), central chemoreceptors reset and hypoxic drive matters more.
  • High-flow O₂ can worsen hypercapnia (mainly via V/Q mismatch and Haldane effect), so target 88–92%.

los.text: Describe the clinical implications of half-life, clearance, volume of distribution, kinetics and AUC
los.html:
Volume of distribution (Vd)
  • Dose / plasma concentration.
  • Large Vd (amiodarone, digoxin) = extensive tissue binding
  • Small Vd (warfarin, gentamicin) = mostly in plasma/ECF.
  • Determines the loading dose = Vd × target concentration.
Clearance (CL)
  • Volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time.
  • Determines the maintenance dose rate = CL × target steady-state concentration. ↓ in renal/hepatic impairment.
Half-life (t½)
  • 0.693 × Vd / CL.
  • Steady state is reached after ~4–5 half-lives, and the drug is ~97% eliminated 4–5 half-lives after stopping.
  • Long t½ → loading dose needed (amiodarone, digoxin).
First-order kineticsConstant fraction eliminated per unit time (most drugs; t½ constant).
Zero-order (saturation) kinetics
  • Constant amount eliminated per unit time once enzymes saturate.
  • Small dose increases → large concentration rises.
  • Examples: phenytoin, ethanol, high-dose aspirin.
AUC(area under concentration–time curve)Total exposure; AUC(oral)/AUC(IV) = bioavailability.
Clinical useDosing intervals, therapeutic drug monitoring (gentamicin, vancomycin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin), dose adjustment in renal impairment.

los.text: Describe the main pathologic mechanisms of common pleuritic diseases, key histopathological features, and associated clinical presentations
los.html:
Pleura
  • Visceral and parietal layers of mesothelium (flat cells with microvilli) over loose connective tissue.
  • Parietal pleura is pain-sensitive (intercostal nerves; central diaphragm via phrenic → shoulder tip pain).
Fibrinous pleuritisExudate of fibrin on the surface → friction rub. Causes: pneumonia, infarction (PE), SLE, uraemia. May organise into fibrous adhesions.
EmpyemaPus in pleural space (complication of pneumonia; neutrophils, organisms). Stages: exudative → fibrinopurulent (loculations) → organising (thick peel, "trapped lung").
Haemothorax (trauma, aortic rupture), chylothorax (thoracic duct injury, lymphoma; milky fluid with triglycerides).
Pleural plaquesHyalinised collagen on parietal pleura, often calcified; marker of asbestos exposure, benign.
Malignant mesothelioma
  • Asbestos (latency 30–40 years).
  • Thick rind encasing the lung
  • Epithelioid, sarcomatoid or biphasic histology
  • Markers calretinin, WT1, CK5/6 (+), BAP1 loss.
  • Presents with pain, breathlessness, unilateral effusion.
  • Compensation: industrial disease.
Metastatic pleural disease (lung, breast, lymphoma, ovary) is far more common than primary mesothelioma.

los.text: Describe the fundamental concepts in psychology and sociology relevant to medicine and health
los.html:
Biopsychosocial model(Engel)Illness results from biological, psychological and social factors interacting; contrasts with the purely biomedical model.
Health vs illness vs diseaseDisease = pathology; illness = subjective experience; sickness = social role.
Sick role(Parsons)Exempt from normal duties and not blamed, but obliged to want to get well and seek competent help.
Illness behaviour(Mechanic)How people perceive, evaluate and act on symptoms. Varies with culture, gender, social class.
Health beliefs and models
  • Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Stages of Change (behaviour change)
  • Illness perceptions (Leventhal's common-sense model: identity, cause, timeline, consequences, control).
Stress and copingLazarus & Folkman transactional model (appraisal); problem- vs emotion-focused coping.
Stigma(Goffman)Discrediting attribute → "spoiled identity" (felt vs enacted stigma).
Social factorsClass, gender, ethnicity, social support. Doctor–patient relationship models: paternalistic, informative, shared decision-making.
